rules.text: Site owner = the one name right before the ending (.co.id, .com, .test). Read the domain from right to left.
The HTTPS padlock only means the connection is encrypted. It doesn't mean the site is honest.
A link's text can be different from its real address. Long-press or right-click the link to see the real address.
Check the sender's address (the domain after @), not just the display name.
Official organizations don't ask for account verification, passwords, or personal data through email links.
Time pressure ("URGENT", "1 hour") and generic greetings ("Dear Customer") are warning signs.
Prizes or lucky draws you never entered are almost always scams.
Real emails: the real domain, greet you by name, and don't pressure you. Don't block without a reason.
Don't open attachments you weren't expecting, especially from unknown senders. Confirm another way first.
A strange request from a coworker's real address can mean their account was taken over. Escalate, then confirm by phone or in person.
Your OTP code is only for you. No IT staff, bank, or courier has the right to ask for it.
A successful login from an unfamiliar location or device after an OTP was shared means the account was taken over: reset the password.
MFA approval requests you didn't ask for must be denied and reported, even if the notifications keep coming.
A login from a new place isn't always bad. Check supporting info (business trips, registered devices) before you act.
Use long passwords, different for each account. A password manager helps you remember them.
What counts is the ending furthest to the right: resi.pdf.apk is an app, not a PDF.
Invitations, delivery receipts, bills, and photos are never .apk, .exe, or .scr files.
Documents that ask you to "Enable Content" (macros) are suspicious.
Dangerous file not opened yet: BLOCK. Already opened on a work device: QUARANTINE the device.
Many failed logins from one IP followed by a success means the password was guessed (brute force).
Two logins from places nobody could travel between in such a short time are called impossible travel.
A login at unusual hours from a new device should be checked with the account owner.
Compare logs with other info (attendance, business trips, helpdesk tickets) before deciding.
Response order: detect, contain, clean up, recover, then report.
Contain the spread first: reset broken-into accounts, quarantine devices, block the attack source.
Escalate when the incident affects many people or important data, or when you're unsure.
